title: Now let your servant go in peace
word: Now let your servant go in peace
tomorrow: if only three things remain, which one wins?

lines: NOW YOU CAN LET ME GO.
cards: Somebody hands you a newborn at a family party. The weight is wrong, lighter than you expected and heavier at the same time. The head smells like warm bread.
Everyone goes a little quiet. In Luke's Gospel an old man named Simeon holds a baby in the Temple, and then says something that sounds alarming: now you can let me go. He isn't sick.
He isn't sad. So why would holding a child make him ready to leave?

teach.h: MY EYES HAVE SEEN THY SALVATION.
teach.b: Listen to the whole sentence, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace; Because my eyes have seen thy salvation." There's the answer, in the word because.
Simeon had been promised he wouldn't die before he saw the Messiah. Now his eyes have seen, and his arms are holding the promise.
Some readers hear a watchman being relieved at the end of a long shift: the thing he was waiting up for has come, and he can rest. It isn't a wish to die.

teach.h: NOT A WISH TO DIE: A PROMISE KEPT.
teach.b: It's the peace of a promise kept. This is the Nunc Dimittis, and the path met it near the beginning, in Camp two.

teach.h: THE LAST PRAYER OF THE DAY.
teach.b: Catholics pray it at Night Prayer, the last prayer of the day, before sleep. Here's the one to tell a friend tonight: the Church ends its day with an old man's song about what his eyes have seen.
Not a list of what's left undone.

That's the senses of it: eyes that have seen, hands that have held. And that's why it sits here, near the summit. Five years on, the song asks a quiet question: what have your eyes seen along the way?

how: Catholics pray Simeon's song, the Nunc Dimittis, every night at Night Prayer (Compline), and remember Simeon at the Presentation of the Lord on February 2.

games.q: what does “now let your servant go in peace” mean?
o: a priest's words sending people home after Mass
a prayer asking God for a peaceful death
Simeon's song: rest, because the promise was seen

p: my eyes have seen thy salvation

s: Simeon's words are a wish to die
they're the peace of a promise kept: "because my eyes have seen thy salvation."
Catholics pray Simeon's song at the end of the day
the Nunc Dimittis belongs to Night Prayer, before sleep.
Simeon was sick when he went to the Temple
Luke says nothing of illness; he was waiting for the promise.

games.q: your grandfather finishes building a backyard bench he promised you as a kid, sits on it, and says, "now i can rest." what's the Simeon reading?
o: he's tired and wants you to leave him alone.
a promise he carried is kept; that's his peace.
he's quietly telling you he's very ill.
games.why: Simeon's peace comes from because: my eyes have seen. a kept promise lets a person rest, the way a watchman rests when the morning comes.

practice: Cup your hands in your lap as if they were holding something small and precious, and feel the weight you imagine there. Bring to mind one thing your eyes have seen on this road that you're glad of.
Then slowly open your hands, palms up, and let them rest that way. If you pray, Simeon's words fit: now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, in peace.

wordCard.voice: Now let your servant go in peace. Simeon's song, the Nunc Dimittis: rest, because the promise has been seen.

orig.note: Latin: now you dismiss. the opening words of Simeon's song, prayed at Night Prayer.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: in peace, not because everything's finished, but because something promised has been seen. Rest well tonight.
